3-1.bio:
St. Eudokia was a Samaritan of Heliopolis in Phoenicia who lived in the early centuries of the Church. Wealthy and famed for her beauty, she was moved to repentance by the words of a monk named Germanos, was baptized, gave her riches to the poor, and entered the monastic life, excelling in fasting and prayer.

Tradition relates that she endured slander and persecution with patience, and at last completed her course as a martyr, beheaded for her confession of Christ. Honored as a model of repentance at the threshold of spring, she is commemorated on March 1.
3-1.name: Eudokia

3-1.bio:
St. Antonina was a Christian woman of Nicaea in Bithynia who suffered during the persecutions of the early fourth century. Brought before the governor for refusing to sacrifice to idols, she was subjected to torture and imprisonment, and tradition relates that she was finally sewn into a sack and cast into a lake.

The Church honors her as a virgin martyr whose steadfastness under torment bore witness to Christ before the pagans of her city. Her memory is kept on March 1.
3-1.desc: Holy Martyr Antonina of Nicaea in Bithynia.
3-1.name: Antonina of Nicaea

3-1.bio:
St. Domnina the New was an ascetic of Syria in the fifth century, known from the writings of Theodoret of Cyrrhus. She lived in a small hut of reeds in her mother's garden, spending her days in prayer and tears, eating only lentils and wearing a rough garment that hid her face.

She received visitors with humility and offered them counsel, and was greatly respected by the ascetics of the region. She reposed in peace, and the Church keeps her memory on March 1.
3-1.desc: Venerable Domnina the New of Syria, ascetic of the fifth century.
3-1.name: Domnina the New

3-1.bio:
St. Paraskevas was a Christian of Trebizond on the Black Sea who lived under Ottoman rule. Tradition relates that he was falsely accused before the Turkish authorities and pressed to deny his faith, but refused every inducement and threat.

He was put to death for his confession of Christ and is numbered among the New Martyrs of the Pontus. His memory is kept on March 1.
3-1.desc: Holy New Martyr Paraskevas of Trebizond, who suffered under the Ottomans.
3-1.name: Paraskevas of Trebizond

3-1.bio:
Sts. Markellos and Antonios were martyrs of Syria whose memory the synaxaria preserve with few details. Tradition relates that they confessed Christ before the pagan authorities and, refusing to renounce Him, were cast into fire and so received the crown of martyrdom.

The Church honors them together on March 1.
3-1.desc: Holy Martyrs Markellos and Antonios of Syria, burned for the faith.
3-1.name: Markellos and Antonios of Syria

3-1.bio:
Sts. Charisios, Nikephoros and Agapios were martyrs of the early Church whose names are preserved in the Greek synaxaria for March 1. Tradition relates that they were put to the sword for their confession of Christ.

Little else of their lives has come down to us, but the Church keeps their memory together on this day.
3-1.desc: Holy Martyrs Charisios, Nikephoros and Agapios.
3-1.name: Charisios, Nikephoros and Agapios

3-1.bio:
St. David (Dewi) was a bishop of the sixth century in Wales, the founder of the monastery at Menevia (now St. Davids) and the most celebrated of the Welsh saints. Tradition relates that he lived with great austerity, drinking only water and laboring with his monks in the fields, and that he preached with such power at the Synod of Brefi that he was acknowledged as chief among the bishops of Wales.

He reposed in peace and is honored as the patron of Wales. His memory is kept on March 1.
3-1.desc: Saint David, Bishop of Menevia, patron and enlightener of Wales.
3-1.name: David of Wales

3-10.bio:
St. Anastasios was a hierarch of the Church of Jerusalem who bore the title of confessor, one who suffered for the faith without denying Christ. The synaxaria preserve little of his life beyond his faithful witness in a time when the Church was tried by heresy and persecution.

The Church honors in him the countless shepherds who guarded the flock of Christ at cost to themselves, their names written more fully in heaven than in the records of men. He is commemorated on March 10.
3-10.name: Anastasios the Confessor

3-10.bio:
St. Kodratos was born near Corinth in the third century, raised, according to tradition, in the wilderness after the death of his mother, and later educated in medicine. He gathered a group of Christian companions, and during the persecution of Decius they were brought before the governor of Corinth, tortured and beheaded.

With him suffered Anektos, Paul, Dionysios, Kyprianos and Kriskes. The Church honors them together on March 10.
3-10.desc: Holy Martyr Kodratos of Corinth and his companions Anektos, Paul, Dionysios, Kyprianos and Kriskes.
3-10.name: Kodratos of Corinth

3-10.bio:
St. Anastasia was a noblewoman of Constantinople in the sixth century who fled the court of the emperor Justinian to escape the jealousy of the empress. She founded a convent near Alexandria, and later, disguised as a eunuch monk, lived for many years in a cave in the desert of Skete under the guidance of Abba Daniel.

Her identity was revealed only at her death. The Church keeps her memory on March 10.
3-10.desc: Venerable Anastasia the Patrician of Alexandria, who lived as a monk in the desert.
3-10.name: Anastasia the Patrician

3-10.bio:
St. Markianos was a martyr whose name the Greek synaxaria record for March 10 with the note that he was stoned to death for his confession of Christ. Nothing further of his life has been preserved.

The Church keeps his memory on this day.
3-10.name: Markianos the Martyr

3-10.bio:
St. Agathon was one of the desert fathers of Egypt whose sayings are preserved in the Apophthegmata. He was known for his discernment, his silence and his love for his neighbor, and tradition relates that he once said he wished he could give a leper his own body in exchange.

He reposed in peace, and the Greek synaxarion keeps his memory on March 10.
3-10.desc: Venerable Agathon of Egypt, desert father.
3-10.name: Agathon the Venerable

3-10.bio:
St. Michael Mavroudis was born in the village of Granitsa in Agrapha and worked as a baker in Thessaloniki under Ottoman rule. Tradition relates that he was accused of speaking against Islam while talking with a Turkish child, was brought before the judge and, refusing to renounce Christ, was burned to death in 1544.

He is numbered among the New Martyrs of Thessaloniki, and his memory is kept on March 10.
3-10.desc: Holy New Martyr Michael Mavroudis of Thessaloniki.
3-10.name: Michael Mavroudis

3-11.bio:
St. Sophronios, Patriarch of Jerusalem, was born in Damascus in the sixth century. A monk and a learned theologian, he traveled the monasteries of the East with his friend John Moschos, and as patriarch he stood firm against the Monothelite heresy, defending the fullness of both the divine and human wills in Christ.

It fell to him to shepherd the Holy City in its darkest hour, when Jerusalem passed under Arab rule in his old age, and he labored to protect his flock and the holy places. A hymnographer of great beauty, he is commemorated on March 11.
3-11.name: Sophronios of Jerusalem

3-11.bio:
St. Theodora was born of the noble Petraliphas family in the thirteenth century and married Michael II Doukas, Despot of Epirus. Slandered and driven from the court by a rival, she endured years of exile with patience until her husband repented and restored her; she then used her position to found churches and monasteries and to care for the poor.

After Michael's death she entered the monastery of St. George in Arta, where she reposed in peace. Her relics rest in the church that now bears her name, and she is the patroness of Arta. Her memory is kept on March 11.
3-11.desc: Saint Theodora, Queen of Arta, patroness of the city.
3-11.name: Theodora of Arta

3-11.bio:
St. Pionios was a presbyter of Smyrna who was arrested with several companions in the third century, on the anniversary of the martyrdom of St. Polycarp. His defense before the authorities, in which he refused every inducement to sacrifice, is preserved in an ancient account of his martyrdom.

He was nailed to a stake and burned, and with him suffered Sabina and others. The Church keeps their memory on March 11.
3-11.desc: Hieromartyr Pionios, presbyter of Smyrna, with the martyr Sabina and companions.
3-11.name: Pionios and Sabina

3-11.bio:
St. George the Newly-Appeared was a monk of Constantinople who lived near the church at Diipion in the tenth century. Tradition relates that he practiced great asceticism and that after his repose his relics were found incorrupt and worked miracles, whence his title.

His memory is kept on March 11.
3-11.desc: Venerable George the Newly-Appeared of Diipion in Constantinople.
3-11.name: George the Newly-Appeared

3-11.bio:
Sts. Trophimos and Thallos were brothers from Stratonikeia in Caria who suffered at Laodicea under the emperor Diocletian. Tradition relates that they were tortured and stoned, and at last crucified, and that they preached Christ from the cross until their death.

The Church keeps their memory on March 11.
3-11.desc: Holy Martyrs Trophimos and Thallos of Laodicea.
3-11.name: Trophimos and Thallos

3-11.bio:
St. Euthymios was born in Novgorod in the late fourteenth century and became a monk in his youth. Chosen Archbishop of Novgorod in 1429, he built churches and monasteries, restored the cathedral of St. Sophia, and was known for his strict life and his love for the monastic rule.

He reposed in 1458 and was glorified for the miracles at his tomb. His memory is kept on March 11.
3-11.desc: Saint Euthymios the Wonderworker, Archbishop of Novgorod.
3-11.name: Euthymios of Novgorod

3-11.bio:
St. Sophronios of Vratsa was born in Kotel in Bulgaria in 1739 and served as a parish priest before becoming Bishop of Vratsa. A disciple of the work of St. Paisios of Hilendar, he labored for the education of the Bulgarian people, copying and translating books and preaching in the vernacular despite persecution by local Ottoman rulers.

He reposed in Bucharest in 1813 and was glorified by the Bulgarian Church in 1964. His memory is kept on March 11.
3-11.desc: Saint Sophronios, Bishop of Vratsa, teacher and enlightener of Bulgaria.
3-11.name: Sophronios of Vratsa

3-12.bio:
St. Theophanes the Confessor was born in Constantinople in the eighth century to a noble family. Renouncing wealth and worldly marriage, he embraced the monastic life and founded a monastery, where he became famed for asceticism and learning; his great chronicle of world history earned him the title Chronographer.

When the iconoclast persecution was renewed, he refused to reject the holy icons, and though aged and ill he was imprisoned and exiled, dying a confessor for the veneration of the icons. He is commemorated on March 12.
3-12.name: Theophanes the Confessor

3-12.bio:
St. Gregory the Dialogist, or Gregory the Great, was born in Rome in the sixth century of a senatorial family, served as prefect of the city, and then gave up everything to become a monk. Against his will he was made Pope of Rome in 590, and he governed the Church with great pastoral wisdom in a time of plague, famine and invasion.

He is called the Dialogist from his book of Dialogues on the lives of the Italian saints, and Orthodox tradition ascribes to him the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts celebrated in Great Lent. He reposed in 604, and his memory is kept on March 12.
3-12.desc: Saint Gregory the Dialogist, Pope of Rome, to whom the Presanctified Liturgy is ascribed.
3-12.name: Gregory the Dialogist

3-12.bio:
St. Symeon the New Theologian was born in Paphlagonia in 949 and, as a young man in Constantinople, came under the guidance of the elder Symeon the Pious of the Studion monastery. He became abbot of the monastery of St. Mamas, where he taught that every Christian is called to a conscious experience of the grace of the Holy Spirit, and he wrote hymns and discourses of extraordinary boldness on the vision of the divine light.

Opposed by some of the hierarchy, he was exiled across the Bosphorus, where he founded a small monastery and reposed in 1022. He is one of only three saints given the title Theologian by the Church. His memory is kept on March 12 and also on October 12.
3-12.desc: Venerable Symeon the New Theologian, mystic and hymnographer of the light of God.
3-12.name: Symeon the New Theologian

3-12.bio:
The righteous Phineas was the son of Eleazar and grandson of Aaron the high priest, whose story is told in the Book of Numbers. His zeal for the law of God in the wilderness turned away the wrath of the Lord from Israel, and God gave him and his descendants the covenant of an everlasting priesthood.

He served as high priest after his father, and the Church keeps his memory on March 12.
3-12.desc: Righteous Phineas, grandson of Aaron, priest of the Old Covenant.
3-12.name: Phineas the Righteous

3-12.bio:
The holy prophet Aaron was the elder brother of Moses and his spokesman before Pharaoh, and by God's command he was consecrated the first high priest of Israel. His rod that budded was kept in the Ark of the Covenant, and the Church sees in it a figure of the Mother of God.

He died on Mount Hor before the entry into the Promised Land. The Greek synaxarion keeps his memory on March 12.
3-12.desc: Holy Prophet Aaron, brother of Moses and first high priest of Israel.
3-12.name: Aaron the Prophet

3-12.bio:
St. Demetrios II, called the Self-Sacrificing, was King of Georgia in the thirteenth century under the domination of the Mongols. When the Mongol khan summoned him under threat of devastating his country, he chose to go, knowing that it meant his death, in order to spare his people.

He was beheaded in 1289 and is honored by the Georgian Church as a righteous king and martyr. His memory is kept on March 12.
3-12.desc: Righteous King Demetrios the Self-Sacrificing of Georgia.
3-12.name: Demetrios of Georgia

3-13.bio:
St. Nikephoros was Patriarch of Constantinople in the early ninth century, during the second wave of iconoclasm. A learned defender of the veneration of the holy icons, he stood against the emperor Leo the Armenian, and for his faithfulness he was deposed from his throne and driven into exile, where he spent his remaining years in prayer and writing until his repose.

After the final triumph of Orthodoxy his relics were returned in honor to Constantinople, an event the Church remembers with joy. He is commemorated on March 13.
3-13.name: Nikephoros of Constantinople

3-13.bio:
St. Publius was Bishop of Athens in the second century, a successor of St. Dionysios the Areopagite according to tradition. He shepherded the Church of Athens in a time of persecution and completed his witness as a martyr.

The Church keeps his memory on March 13.
3-13.name: Publius of Athens

3-13.bio:
Sts. Africanus, Publius and Terence were martyrs of Carthage in North Africa who suffered in the persecution of Decius in the third century. Refusing to sacrifice to idols, they were tortured and beheaded together with a number of companions.

The Church honors them on March 13.
3-13.desc: Holy Martyrs Africanus, Publius and Terence of Carthage.
3-13.name: Africanus, Publius and Terence

3-13.bio:
St. Christina was a Christian woman of Persia who suffered for her faith in the fourth century. Tradition relates that she was scourged to death for refusing to renounce Christ.

The Church keeps her memory on March 13.
3-13.desc: Holy Martyr Christina of Persia, scourged to death for Christ.
3-13.name: Christina of Persia

3-13.bio:
St. Euphrasia is a venerable woman whose name the Greek synaxaria record for March 13 with the note that she reposed in peace. Nothing further of her life has been preserved.

The Church honors her on this day.
3-13.desc: Venerable Euphrasia, who reposed in peace.
3-13.name: Euphrasia the Venerable

3-13.bio:
St. Hypomone was born Helen Dragas, daughter of a Serbian prince, and became the wife of the emperor Manuel II Palaiologos and mother of the last two emperors of Byzantium, John VIII and Constantine XI. A woman of deep piety, she was the support of her family through the final years of the empire.

After her husband's death she was tonsured a nun with the name Hypomone, meaning Patience, and lived in the monastery of Kyra Martha in Constantinople until her repose in 1450. Her memory is kept on March 13 and on May 29.
3-13.desc: Venerable Hypomone, the former Empress Helen Dragas, mother of the last emperors of Byzantium.
3-13.name: Hypomone

3-13.bio:
St. Marios was a bishop of Sebaste in Armenia whose name is preserved in the Greek synaxaria for March 13. Tradition relates that he governed his flock in holiness and reposed in peace.

The Church keeps his memory on this day.
3-13.name: Marios of Sebaste

3-14.bio:
St. Benedict was born in Nursia in Italy in the late fifth century. Leaving his studies in Rome to flee the corruption of the world, he lived first as a hermit in a cave at Subiaco, and later founded the great monastery of Monte Cassino. His Rule for monks, marked by prayer, labor, moderation, and obedience, shaped the whole monastic life of the Christian West.

Revered as the father of Western monasticism, he reposed in the sixth century and is honored throughout the Church, East and West alike. He is commemorated on March 14.
3-14.name: Benedict of Nursia

3-14.bio:
St. Euschemon was Bishop of Lampsakos on the Hellespont in the ninth century. A friend and correspondent of St. Theodore the Studite, he suffered imprisonment and exile for his defense of the holy icons under the iconoclast emperor Theophilos.

He reposed in exile, and the Church honors him as a confessor on March 14.
3-14.desc: Saint Euschemon the Confessor, Bishop of Lampsakos.
3-14.name: Euschemon of Lampsakos

3-14.bio:
St. Alexander was a priest of Pydna in Macedonia who suffered in the persecution of Maximian at the beginning of the fourth century. Tradition relates that he rebuked the emperor for his idolatry and was beheaded near Thessaloniki.

The Church of Macedonia keeps his memory on March 14.
3-14.desc: Hieromartyr Alexander, priest of Pydna in Macedonia.
3-14.name: Alexander of Pydna

3-14.bio:
Sts. Basil and Euphrasios are martyrs whose names the Greek synaxaria record for March 14. Tradition relates that they confessed Christ and were put to death for the faith.

The Church keeps their memory together on this day.
3-14.name: Basil and Euphrasios

3-14.bio:
St. Theognostos was a Greek by birth, sent from Constantinople in 1328 to succeed St. Peter as Metropolitan of Kiev and All Russia. He fixed his residence in Moscow, defended the Church against the demands of the Mongol khans, and built up the churches of the growing city.

He reposed in 1353 and was buried beside St. Peter in the Dormition Cathedral of the Kremlin. His memory is kept on March 14.
3-14.desc: Saint Theognostos the Greek, Metropolitan of Kiev and All Russia.
3-14.name: Theognostos of Kiev

3-14.bio:
St. Rostislav, baptized Michael, was Prince of Smolensk and later Great Prince of Kiev in the twelfth century. He founded the diocese of Smolensk, built churches, and was known for his justice, his love of peace among the quarreling princes, and his generosity to monasteries.

He reposed in 1167 on his way back to Kiev, and his memory is kept on March 14.
3-14.desc: Right-believing Great Prince Rostislav of Kiev and Smolensk.
3-14.name: Rostislav of Kiev

3-15.bio:
St. Agapios was a martyr who suffered at Caesarea in Palestine during the great persecutions at the beginning of the fourth century. Together with several companions, he confessed Christ before the governor and refused every inducement to sacrifice to the idols, and so was put to death for the faith.

His name, which means beloved, befits one who loved Christ more than life itself. The Church commemorates St. Agapios and his fellow martyrs on March 15.
3-15.name: Agapios

3-15.bio:
St. Aristoboulos was one of the Seventy Apostles, greeted by St. Paul in the Epistle to the Romans and, according to tradition, the brother of St. Barnabas. He accompanied St. Paul in his travels and was sent to preach the Gospel in Britain, where he is honored as its first bishop.

Tradition relates that he suffered much from the pagans but established the Church there before reposing in peace. His memory is kept on March 15 and on October 31.
3-15.desc: Holy Apostle Aristoboulos of the Seventy, Bishop of Britain.
3-15.name: Aristoboulos the Apostle

3-15.bio:
St. Manuel was born in Sfakia in Crete and, taken captive as a child, was forced to accept Islam; escaping to the island of Mykonos, he returned to the Christian faith and lived as a married man. Tradition relates that he was later recognized and denounced on Chios, and when he refused to return to Islam he was beheaded in 1792.

He is numbered among the New Martyrs of Crete, and his memory is kept on March 15.
3-15.desc: Holy New Martyr Manuel of Sfakia in Crete, martyred on Chios.
3-15.name: Manuel of Sfakia

3-15.bio:
St. Nikandros was a Christian of Egypt, a physician by profession, who suffered in the persecution of Diocletian. Tradition relates that he was arrested for gathering and burying the bodies of the martyrs, and that he was flayed alive and beheaded for his confession of Christ.

The Church keeps his memory on March 15.
3-15.desc: Holy Martyr Nikandros of Egypt, physician.
3-15.name: Nikandros of Egypt

3-15.bio:
St. Agapios was a monk of the skete of Kolitsou, near Vatopedi on Mount Athos, in the fifteenth century. Tradition relates that he was carried off by pirates and held as a slave for many years, and that he was miraculously freed by the Mother of God and returned to his elder, who sent him back to convert his former master.

His master and his sons received baptism and became monks with him on the Holy Mountain. The Church honors them together on March 15 and on March 1.
3-15.desc: Venerable Agapios of the Skete of Kolitsou on Mount Athos, with his four disciples.
3-15.name: Agapios of Kolitsou

3-15.bio:
St. John was an ascetic of Egypt who, according to tradition, lived for many years in a dry well near a village, practicing prayer and fasting in complete solitude. He was known for his humility and for the gift of foresight.

He reposed in peace, and the Greek synaxarion keeps his memory on March 15 and again on March 30.
3-15.desc: Venerable John who lived in a well.
3-15.name: John in the Well

3-16.bio:
St. Christodoulos was a monk of the eleventh century, born in Asia Minor, who lived the ascetic life in various monasteries of the East before receiving from the emperor the island of Patmos, where St. John received the Revelation. There he founded the great Monastery of St. John the Theologian, which crowns the island to this day.

Honored as a wonderworker in his lifetime and after his repose, he made Patmos one of the enduring lamps of Orthodox monasticism. His relics rest at his monastery, and he is commemorated on March 16.
3-16.name: Christodoulos of Patmos

3-16.bio:
St. Sabinus was a Christian of Hermopolis in Egypt who, during the persecution of Diocletian, hid with a group of believers in a hut outside the city. Betrayed by a beggar whom he had helped, he was arrested, tortured and drowned in the Nile.

The Church keeps his memory on March 16.
3-16.desc: Holy Martyr Sabinus of Hermopolis in Egypt.
3-16.name: Sabinus of Egypt

3-16.bio:
St. Romanos was a martyr of Parion on the Hellespont whose name the Greek synaxaria record for March 16. Tradition relates that he confessed Christ before the pagan authorities and was put to death by the sword.

The Church keeps his memory on this day.
3-16.name: Romanos of Parion

3-16.bio:
St. Julian was a young Christian of Anazarbus in Cilicia, of a senatorial family, who suffered under Diocletian. Tradition relates that after a year of tortures he was sewn into a sack filled with sand and venomous creatures and cast into the sea, and that his body was recovered and later brought to Antioch.

St. John Chrysostom honored him with a homily. The Greek synaxarion keeps his memory on March 16.
3-16.desc: Holy Martyr Julian of Anazarbus in Cilicia, cast into the sea in a sack.
3-16.name: Julian of Cilicia

3-16.bio:
St. Alexander was Bishop of Rome in the early second century, in the days of the emperor Hadrian according to tradition. He is remembered as a hieromartyr who confessed Christ and was put to death for the faith.

The Church keeps his memory on March 16.
3-16.name: Alexander of Rome

3-16.bio:
St. Aninas was born in Chalcedon and lived as an ascetic near the Euphrates in Syria, in the fourth or fifth century. Tradition relates that he was granted great gifts of healing and prophecy, that wild animals obeyed him, and that many came to him for counsel.

He reposed in peace at a great age, and the Church keeps his memory on March 16 and March 18.
3-16.desc: Venerable Aninas the Wonderworker of the Euphrates.
3-16.name: Aninas the Wonderworker

3-17.bio:
St. Alexios, the Man of God, was the son of a noble Roman family. On the night of his wedding he secretly left his home, choosing poverty for the sake of Christ, and lived for years as a beggar in the East, spending his days in fasting and prayer at the doors of the church.

Tradition relates that he returned at last to his father's house, where he lived unrecognized as a poor stranger, enduring contempt with patience; only at his death was it revealed who he was. A beloved image of hidden holiness, he is commemorated on March 17.
3-17.name: Alexios Man of God

3-17.bio:
St. Patrick was born in Roman Britain in the late fourth century and as a youth was carried off by raiders to Ireland, where he tended sheep as a slave and learned to pray. After escaping and being ordained, he returned to Ireland as a bishop and spent the rest of his life preaching the Gospel, baptizing kings and people, and founding churches and monasteries.

His own short Confession survives, full of humility and gratitude. He reposed in the fifth century and is honored as the apostle of Ireland. His memory is kept on March 17.
3-17.desc: Saint Patrick, Bishop of Armagh, enlightener of Ireland.
3-17.name: Patrick of Ireland

3-17.bio:
St. Theosteriktos was abbot of the monastery of Pelekete in Bithynia in the eighth century, during the iconoclast persecution of Constantine Copronymos. Tradition relates that when soldiers attacked the monastery on Holy Thursday, many of the monks were killed and he himself was tortured and had his nose cut off for his defense of the holy icons.

He survived to govern his monastery for many years and reposed in peace. The Church honors him as a confessor on March 17.
3-17.desc: Venerable Theosteriktos the Confessor, abbot of the Pelekete monastery.
3-17.name: Theosteriktos the Confessor

3-17.bio:
St. Marinos was a soldier who suffered for Christ during the Roman persecutions. Tradition relates that he was denounced as a Christian by a rival who wanted his position, and that when he confessed the faith openly he was tortured and beheaded.

The Church keeps his memory on March 17.
3-17.name: Marinos the Martyr

3-17.bio:
The righteous Lazarus of Bethany, brother of Martha and Mary, was raised from the dead by the Lord four days after his burial, as the Gospel of John relates. Tradition holds that he later fled the persecution of the Jews and came to Cyprus, where he was made Bishop of Kition by the Apostles and lived for thirty more years.

His relics were translated to Constantinople in the ninth century. Besides Lazarus Saturday before Palm Sunday, the Church keeps his memory on March 17 and October 17.
3-17.desc: Righteous Lazarus the Four-Days-Dead, friend of Christ and Bishop of Kition.
3-17.name: Lazarus the Friend of Christ

3-17.bio:
St. Paul was a monk who suffered during the iconoclast persecution of the eighth century. Tradition relates that he refused to trample on an icon of Christ when commanded, and that he was burned to death for his confession.

The Church keeps his memory on March 17.
3-17.desc: Holy Monk-Martyr Paul, burned for the holy icons.
3-17.name: Paul the Monk-Martyr

3-17.bio:
St. Makarios was born of a noble family near Tver in the fifteenth century and, after the death of his wife, became a monk. Seeking solitude, he settled in a forest by the Volga, where disciples gathered and the monastery of Kalyazin grew up around him.

He was known for his humility, working with his own hands and wearing patched clothing, and for the miracles at his tomb after his repose in 1483. His memory is kept on March 17.
3-17.desc: Venerable Makarios, abbot of Kalyazin, wonderworker.
3-17.name: Makarios of Kalyazin

3-18.bio:
St. Cyril was Archbishop of Jerusalem in the fourth century, a gentle and learned shepherd of the Holy City. His famous Catechetical Lectures, delivered to those preparing for baptism, remain one of the treasures of the ancient Church, setting forth the faith and the holy mysteries with clarity and warmth.

For his defense of the Orthodox faith against Arianism he was driven from his throne several times, spending years in exile before being restored. He reposed in peace near the end of the fourth century and is commemorated on March 18.
3-18.desc: Archbishop of Jerusalem and great catechist.
3-18.name: Cyril of Jerusalem

3-18.bio:
Sts. Trophimos and Eukarpion were soldiers of Nicomedia in the persecution of Diocletian, employed in hunting down Christians. Tradition relates that they were converted by a vision on the road, released the prisoners in their charge, and confessed Christ before the governor.

They were burned alive, and the Church keeps their memory on March 18.
3-18.desc: Holy Martyrs Trophimos and Eukarpion of Nicomedia, former persecutors.
3-18.name: Trophimos and Eukarpion

3-18.bio:
The Greek synaxarion for March 18 commemorates ten thousand martyrs who confessed Christ and were put to the sword during the persecutions of the early Church. The place and time of their martyrdom have not been preserved.

The Church honors the whole company on this day.
3-18.desc: The Ten Thousand Holy Martyrs, who were put to the sword.
3-18.name: Ten Thousand Martyrs

3-18.bio:
St. Ananias is a venerable father whom the Greek synaxaria commemorate on March 18 with the note that he was a wonderworker who reposed in peace. Nothing further of his life has been preserved.

The Church honors him on this day.
3-18.desc: Venerable Ananias the Wonderworker, who reposed in peace.
3-18.name: Ananias the Wonderworker

3-18.bio:
St. Edward became King of England in 975 while still a youth and reigned for only a few years. Tradition relates that he was murdered at Corfe in 978 through the plotting of his stepmother, and that miracles soon followed at his grave, so that he was honored as a martyr throughout England.

His relics rest today in an Orthodox church at Brookwood in England. His memory is kept on March 18.
3-18.desc: Saint Edward the Martyr, King of England.
3-18.name: Edward of England

3-18.bio:
St. Cyril was a monk sent to Astrakhan on the lower Volga in the sixteenth century, soon after the city came under Russian rule, to establish a monastery of the Holy Trinity. Tradition relates that he was respected even by the Tatars for his humility and honesty, and that he labored for the spread of the faith in the region.

He reposed in 1576, and his memory is kept on March 18.
3-18.desc: Venerable Cyril, abbot of the Trinity monastery of Astrakhan.
3-18.name: Cyril of Astrakhan

3-19.bio:
Sts. Chrysanthos and Daria were martyrs of Rome in the third century. Chrysanthos, the son of a pagan noble, came to faith in Christ through the reading of the Scriptures; when his father arranged his marriage to Daria, a learned pagan woman, Chrysanthos won her to the faith, and the two lived in purity, devoting themselves to prayer and to bringing others to Christ.

Denounced as Christians, they endured tortures and were put to death together for their confession. The Church commemorates this holy pair on March 19.
3-19.name: Chrysanthos and Daria

3-19.bio:
St. Claudius was a tribune in Rome who was charged with the torture of Sts. Chrysanthos and Daria. Moved by their steadfastness and by the miracles he witnessed, he came to faith in Christ together with his wife Hilaria, their sons Jason and Maurus, and many of his soldiers.

Claudius was drowned in the sea, his sons and soldiers were beheaded, and Hilaria, who went to pray at their graves, was seized and died a martyr. The Church keeps their memory with Chrysanthos and Daria on March 19.
3-19.desc: Holy Martyrs Claudius the Tribune, his wife Hilaria and their sons Jason and Maurus.
3-19.name: Claudius and Hilaria

3-19.bio:
St. Pancharios was a Christian of Germanicia in Asia Minor who served at the court of Diocletian in Nicomedia. Tradition relates that out of fear he at first denied Christ, but that a letter from his mother and sister brought him to repentance; he confessed the faith before the emperor and was beheaded.

The Church keeps his memory on March 19.
3-19.name: Pancharios the Martyr

3-19.bio:
Sts. Diodoros the presbyter and Marianos the deacon are martyrs of the early Church commemorated together in the Greek synaxaria on March 19. Tradition relates that they were shut up in a cave and died there for their confession of Christ.

The Church keeps their memory on this day.
3-19.desc: Hieromartyrs Diodoros the Presbyter and Marianos the Deacon.
3-19.name: Diodoros and Marianos

3-19.bio:
St. Demetrios Tornaras was a New Martyr of the Ottoman period. Tradition relates that he was accused before the Turkish authorities and, when pressed to accept Islam, refused and was beheaded in Constantinople in 1564.

His memory is kept on March 19.
3-19.name: Demetrios Tornaras

3-19.bio:
St. Innocent was a monk of the Kirillov monastery who became a disciple of St. Nilus of Sora and accompanied him on his journey to Mount Athos. Returning to the north of Russia, he founded a skete in the forest of Komel near Vologda, living according to the way of hesychast prayer taught by his elder.

He reposed in 1521, and his memory is kept on March 19.
3-19.desc: Venerable Innocent of Komel and Vologda, disciple of Saint Nilus of Sora.
3-19.name: Innocent of Komel

3-2.bio:
St. Efthalia was a virgin martyr of Sicily in the early centuries of the Church. Tradition relates that she came to faith in Christ together with her mother, and that when her pagan brother raged against her confession she would not renounce the Lord, and so gave her life for the faith.

The synaxaria preserve little else of her story, but the Church has kept her memory as one of the pure virgin martyrs whose steadfastness shone within her own household. She is commemorated on March 2.
3-2.name: Efthalia

3-2.bio:
St. Theodotos was Bishop of Kyrenia in Cyprus in the early fourth century. During the persecution of Licinius he was arrested and subjected to severe tortures for his confession of Christ, enduring them with such courage that many pagans who witnessed his sufferings came to faith.

When St. Constantine granted peace to the Church he was released, returned to his flock, and reposed in peace some years later. The Church honors him as a hieromartyr and confessor on March 2.
3-2.desc: Hieromartyr Theodotos, Bishop of Kyrenia in Cyprus, confessor under Licinius.
3-2.name: Theodotos of Kyrenia

3-2.bio:
St. Nicholas Planas was born on the island of Naxos in 1851 and served as a parish priest in Athens for more than fifty years, until his repose in 1932. Of small stature and simple learning, he celebrated the Divine Liturgy nearly every day, commemorating thousands of names, and was loved by the poor of the city for his gentleness and charity.

Among those who attended his all-night vigils were the writers Alexandros Papadiamantis and Alexandros Moraitidis. He was glorified by the Ecumenical Patriarchate in 1992, and his memory is kept on March 2.
3-2.desc: Saint Nicholas Planas, the humble priest of Athens.
3-2.name: Nicholas Planas

3-2.bio:
St. Kointos was a Christian of Phrygia in the third century, remembered for his generosity to the poor and for the gift of healing. Tradition relates that he was seized during a persecution, but that an earthquake dispersed his tormentors and he was set free; later he was again tortured, and his legs were broken, yet he was healed and lived on for many years.

He reposed in peace after a life of charity and miracles, and the Church honors him as a confessor on March 2.
3-2.desc: Saint Kointos (Quintus) the Confessor and Wonderworker of Phrygia.
3-2.name: Kointos the Confessor

3-2.bio:
Sts. Nestor and Tribimios were Christians of Perge in Pamphylia who suffered in the persecution of Decius in the third century. Brought before the governor, they confessed Christ openly, were tortured, and were beheaded.

The Church keeps their memory together on March 2.
3-2.desc: Holy Martyrs Nestor and Tribimios of Perge in Pamphylia.
3-2.name: Nestor and Tribimios

3-2.bio:
St. Joachim, known affectionately as Papoulakis, was born on the island of Ithaca in 1786. As a young man he fled to Mount Athos, where he lived for many years in obedience and prayer at the monastery of Vatopedi. Returning to Ithaca, he devoted himself to the poor, to preaching, and to consoling the islanders, and was known for foretelling events and for his love of children.

He reposed in 1868 and was glorified by the Ecumenical Patriarchate in 1998. His memory is kept on March 2.
3-2.desc: Venerable Joachim of Ithaca, called Papoulakis, ascetic of Mount Athos and Ithaca.
3-2.name: Joachim of Ithaca

3-2.bio:
Sts. Andronikos and Athanasia were a married couple of Antioch in the fifth century. After the death of their two children they gave away their property and went to Egypt, where each embraced the monastic life, Andronikos among the fathers of Skete and Athanasia disguised as a monk.

Tradition relates that they later lived for years in the same cell without Andronikos recognizing his wife, and that her identity was revealed only at her death. The Greek synaxarion commemorates them on March 2 as well as on October 9.
3-2.desc: Righteous Andronikos and his wife Athanasia of Antioch, ascetics of Egypt.
3-2.name: Andronikos and Athanasia

3-20.bio:
The Iveron Icon of the Theotokos, the Portaitissa or Gate-Keeper, is one of the most venerated icons of the Mother of God. According to tradition, during the iconoclast persecutions a pious widow entrusted the icon to the sea; generations later it appeared in a pillar of light off Mount Athos and was received by the monks of the Iveron Monastery, where it has remained for a thousand years as protectress of the Holy Mountain.

Many miracles are ascribed to the Portaitissa, and copies of the icon are venerated throughout the Orthodox world. The Church commemorates the icon on this day with thanksgiving to the Theotokos.
3-20.desc: Feast of the Iveron Icon of the Theotokos.
3-20.name: Mother of God of Iveron

3-20.bio:
On this day the Church remembers the monks of the Great Lavra of St. Savva in the Judean desert who were killed by Arab raiders, most famously in the attack of the year 796. The raiders demanded the monastery's treasures; when the fathers answered that they had nothing but their prayers, many were shut in a cave and suffocated with smoke, and others were cut down.

An eyewitness account was written by Stephen of Mar Saba. The Church honors the martyred fathers on March 20.
3-20.desc: Holy Fathers slain by the Saracens at the Monastery of Saint Savva in Palestine.
3-20.name: Fathers of Saint Savva

3-20.bio:
St. Myron was a young tailor of Heraklion in Crete who lived under Ottoman rule. Tradition relates that he was falsely accused by Turks of having promised to accept Islam, and when he refused to do so he was imprisoned, tortured and hanged in 1793.

He is numbered among the New Martyrs of Crete, and his memory is kept on March 20.
3-20.desc: Holy New Martyr Myron of Heraklion in Crete.
3-20.name: Myron of Crete

3-20.bio:
St. Niketas was Bishop of Apollonias in Bithynia in the ninth century. For his defense of the holy icons during the second period of iconoclasm he was persecuted and driven from his see.

He reposed in exile, and the Church honors him as a confessor on March 20.
3-20.desc: Saint Niketas the Confessor, Bishop of Apollonias in Bithynia.
3-20.name: Niketas of Apollonias

3-20.bio:
The seven virgin martyrs Alexandria, Claudia, Euphrasia, Matrona, Juliana, Euphemia and Theodosia were Christians of Amisos on the Black Sea who suffered in the persecution of Maximian. Brought before the governor, they confessed Christ and endured tortures, and were burned to death together.

The Church keeps their memory on March 20.
3-20.desc: Holy Virgin Martyrs Alexandria, Claudia, Euphrasia, Matrona, Juliana, Euphemia and Theodosia of Amisos.
3-20.name: Seven Virgin Martyrs of Amisos

3-20.bio:
Sts. Rodianos, Akylas the Eparch, Lollion and Emmanuel are martyrs whose names the Greek synaxaria record together for March 20. Tradition relates that they confessed Christ and were put to death for the faith.

The Church keeps their memory on this day.
3-20.desc: Holy Martyrs Rodianos, Akylas the Eparch, Lollion and Emmanuel.
3-20.name: Rodianos, Akylas, Lollion and Emmanuel

3-20.bio:
St. Cuthbert was a monk of Melrose and later prior and bishop of Lindisfarne in Northumbria in the seventh century. He traveled tirelessly to preach in remote villages, lived for years as a hermit on the island of Farne, and was known for his gentleness, his love of animals, and his miracles.

He reposed in 687, and his body was found incorrupt years later; his relics rest in Durham. He is one of the most beloved saints of England, and his memory is kept on March 20.
3-20.desc: Venerable Cuthbert, Bishop of Lindisfarne, wonderworker of Britain.
3-20.name: Cuthbert of Lindisfarne

3-21.bio:
St. Thomas, called the Twin, was one of the Twelve Apostles of the Lord. It was he who said he would not believe unless he touched the wounds of the risen Christ, and who, beholding the Lord eight days after Pascha, made the great confession, my Lord and my God. His honest doubt became for all generations a confirmation of the Resurrection.

According to ancient tradition he carried the Gospel to the East, preaching as far as India, where he completed his apostolic labors as a martyr. He is commemorated on March 21.
3-21.name: Thomas the Apostle

3-21.bio:
St. James was a monk of the Studion monastery who became Bishop of Catania in Sicily in the ninth century. For his defense of the holy icons during the second iconoclast persecution he was subjected to hunger, imprisonment and exile.

He reposed in exile, and the Church honors him as a confessor on March 21.
3-21.desc: Saint James the Confessor, Bishop of Catania.
3-21.name: James of Catania

3-21.bio:
St. Thomas was Patriarch of Constantinople at the beginning of the seventh century, in the reign of the emperor Phokas. Tradition relates that he was a man of great virtue who, troubled by a sign foretelling calamities for the Church, asked St. Theodore of Sykeon to pray that he might die before seeing them, and reposed soon after.

His memory is kept on March 21.
3-21.name: Thomas of Constantinople

3-21.bio:
St. Serapion was a friend of St. Anthony the Great and St. Athanasius, and became Bishop of Thmuis in the Nile delta in the fourth century. A learned man, he defended the Orthodox faith against the Arians and wrote a treatise on the divinity of the Holy Spirit; an ancient liturgical prayer book bears his name.

He suffered exile for the faith and reposed in peace. The Greek synaxarion keeps his memory on March 21.
3-21.desc: Saint Serapion of Sidon, Bishop of Thmuis in Egypt.
3-21.name: Serapion of Sidon

3-21.bio:
Sts. Philemon and Domninos were Christians of Rome who, according to tradition, traveled through Italy preaching the Gospel. They were arrested, tortured and beheaded for their confession of Christ.

The Church keeps their memory on March 21.
3-21.desc: Holy Martyrs Philemon and Domninos of Rome.
3-21.name: Philemon and Domninos

3-21.bio:
St. Seraphim of Vyritsa was born in 1866 and was a successful merchant in St. Petersburg before he and his wife entered monastic life. He became the spiritual father of the Alexander Nevsky Lavra and, after its closure, lived at Vyritsa near St. Petersburg, where he received countless visitors and prayed for Russia through the years of persecution and war.

He reposed in 1949 and was glorified by the Russian Church in 2000. His memory is kept on March 21.
3-21.desc: Venerable Seraphim of Vyritsa, elder and wonderworker of Russia.
3-21.name: Seraphim of Vyritsa

3-22.bio:
St. Basil was a priest of the church of Ancyra in Asia Minor in the fourth century. A faithful shepherd who strengthened his flock against both paganism and heresy, he was seized during the reign of Julian the Apostate, when the emperor sought to restore the worship of idols. Refusing to deny Christ, he endured cruel tortures and completed his course as a martyr around the year 362.

His fearless answers before his persecutors are preserved in the tradition of the Church, which honors him as a model of priestly courage. He is commemorated on March 22.
3-22.name: Basil of Ancyra

3-22.bio:
Sts. Kalliniki and Basilissa were wealthy Christian women of Rome who used their means to visit and support the imprisoned confessors during the persecutions. Denounced for this, they were arrested and, confessing Christ before the governor, were beheaded.

The Church keeps their memory on March 22.
3-22.desc: Holy Martyrs Kalliniki and Basilissa of Rome.
3-22.name: Kalliniki and Basilissa

3-22.bio:
St. Euthymios was born in Demetsana in the Peloponnese in the eighteenth century and, while living in Romania, in a moment of weakness accepted Islam. Filled with remorse, he went to Mount Athos, was received back into the Church at the skete of St. John the Forerunner, and prepared himself for martyrdom.

He returned to Constantinople, openly confessed Christ before the Turkish authorities, and was beheaded in 1814. His memory is kept on March 22, together with his companions Ignatios and Akakios on May 1.
3-22.desc: Holy New Martyr Euthymios of the Peloponnese, monk of the Skete of Prodromou on Athos.
3-22.name: Euthymios of the Peloponnese

3-22.bio:
St. Drosis was, according to tradition, the daughter of the emperor Trajan. Moved by the example of five Christian virgins who were secretly gathering and burying the bodies of the martyrs in Rome, she joined them in their work and came to faith in Christ.

The five virgins were put to death in boiling copper, and Drosis, after baptizing herself in the name of the Trinity, also gave her life for Christ. St. John Chrysostom honored her with a homily. The Church keeps their memory on March 22.
3-22.desc: Holy Martyr Drosis, daughter of the emperor Trajan, with five virgins.
3-22.name: Drosis and the Five Virgins

3-22.bio:
St. Sophia is a monk-martyr whose name the Greek synaxaria record for March 22. Tradition relates that she lived in the monastic life and was put to death for her confession of Christ.

The Church keeps her memory on this day.
3-22.name: Sophia the Monk-Martyr

3-22.bio:
On this day the Church of Rhodes gathers in one commemoration all the saints connected with the island, from the early martyrs and bishops through the New Martyrs of the Ottoman period.

The synaxis was established in recent years by the local metropolis and is kept on March 22.
3-22.desc: Synaxis of all the saints of the island of Rhodes.
3-22.name: Synaxis of the Saints of Rhodes

3-23.bio:
St. Nikon lived in the third century. A soldier's son who came to faith in Christ, he was baptized, embraced the monastic life, and was later made a bishop, gathering many disciples whom he guided in prayer and asceticism. Fleeing persecution, he settled with them in Sicily.

There, during the persecutions of that age, he was seized together with one hundred ninety-nine of his disciples, and all of them were put to death for their confession of Christ, the shepherd suffering last of all. The Church commemorates St. Nikon and his disciples on March 23.
3-23.desc: Holy Martyr Nikon of Sicily and his 199 disciples.
3-23.name: Nikon

3-23.bio:
St. Luke was born in Adrianople in Thrace at the end of the eighteenth century and, as a boy, was carried off by Turks and forced to accept Islam. Escaping to Mount Athos, he returned to Christ and became a monk at the skete of St. Anne, and later, longing for martyrdom, went to Mytilene.

There he confessed Christ before the Turkish judge and was hanged in 1802. His memory is kept on March 23.
3-23.desc: Holy New Martyr Luke of Adrianople, monk of Mount Athos, martyred on Mytilene.
3-23.name: Luke of Adrianople

3-23.bio:
St. Dometios is a martyr whose name the Greek synaxaria record for March 23 with the note that he completed his witness by the sword. Nothing further of his life has been preserved.

The Church keeps his memory on this day.
3-23.name: Dometios the Martyr

3-23.bio:
St. Pachomios the Anchorite is a venerable father whom the Greek synaxaria commemorate on March 23 with the note that he reposed in peace. Nothing further of his life has come down to us.

The Church honors him on this day.
3-23.desc: Venerable Pachomios the Anchorite, who reposed in peace.
3-23.name: Pachomios the Anchorite

3-23.bio:
St. Nikon was one of the first companions of St. Anthony of the Kiev Caves in the eleventh century, a priest who tonsured many of the early monks of the Lavra, including St. Theodosius. He spent some years in a monastery he founded near the Sea of Azov and returned to become abbot of the Caves, where he adorned the great church with icons.

He reposed in 1088, and his memory is kept on March 23.
3-23.desc: Venerable Nikon, abbot of the Kiev Caves Lavra.
3-23.name: Nikon of the Kiev Caves

3-24.bio:
St. Artemon is honored as one of the earliest bishops of the Church, shepherd of Seleucia in Asia Minor in apostolic times. Tradition associates him with the first generation of those who received the Gospel from the Apostles and gave their lives to establishing the Church among the pagans.

The synaxaria preserve little of his life beyond his faithful episcopal service, but his memory endures as one of the quiet founders on whom the Church was built. He is commemorated on March 24.
3-24.name: Artemon, Bishop of Seleucia

3-24.bio:
St. Artemon was a presbyter of Laodicea in Syria who suffered in the persecution of Diocletian. Tradition relates that he was arrested at a great age by the governor Patrikios, endured tortures with wonderful patience, and was finally beheaded.

The Church keeps his memory on March 24, together with his namesake, the Bishop of Seleucia.
3-24.desc: Hieromartyr Artemon, presbyter of Laodicea in Syria.
3-24.name: Artemon of Laodicea

3-24.bio:
St. Parthenios III, called Parthenakis, was Patriarch of Constantinople in the seventeenth century. Accused before the Ottoman authorities of conspiring with foreign powers and refusing to accept Islam to save his life, he was hanged in 1657.

He is honored as a hieromartyr, and his memory is kept on March 24.
3-24.desc: Hieromartyr Parthenios III, Patriarch of Constantinople, hanged by the Ottomans.
3-24.name: Parthenios III of Constantinople

3-24.bio:
St. Zacharias the Recluse was an ascetic who, according to tradition, was the son of a monk of Skete and grew up in the desert of Egypt, where he was known for his humility and for the gift of tears. The Church honors him on March 24 along with a second Zacharias, an ascetic of the Kiev Caves.

Both reposed in peace, and their memory is kept on this day.
3-24.desc: Venerable Zacharias the Recluse, ascetic of Egypt.
3-24.name: Zacharias the Recluse

3-24.bio:
St. Martin of Thebes is a venerable father whose name the Greek synaxaria record for March 24 with the note that he reposed in peace. Nothing further of his life has been preserved.

The Church honors him on this day.
3-24.desc: Venerable Martin of Thebes, who reposed in peace.
3-24.name: Martin of Thebes

3-24.bio:
The Greek synaxarion for March 24 commemorates eight martyrs of Caesarea in Palestine who confessed Christ during the persecutions and were put to death together. Their names have not been preserved.

The Church honors them as one company on this day.
3-24.desc: The Eight Holy Martyrs of Caesarea in Palestine.
3-24.name: Eight Martyrs of Caesarea

3-25.bio:
The Great Feast of the Annunciation commemorates the day the Archangel Gabriel was sent to the Virgin Mary in Nazareth to announce that she would conceive and bear the Son of God. Her humble acceptance as the handmaid of the Lord opened the way for the Incarnation, and at that moment the Word of God took flesh in her womb.

Celebrated on March 25, nine months before the Nativity of Christ, the Annunciation is one of the most beloved feasts of the Theotokos. For the Greek people the day carries a double joy, as it also marks the beginning of the struggle for independence in 1821.
3-25.desc: The Annunciation of the Most Holy Theotokos — Archangel Gabriel announces the Incarnation.
3-25.name: Annunciation

3-25.bio:
St. Sennouphios was an ascetic of Egypt in the fourth century, famed for his miracles and called the Sign-Bearer. Tradition relates that the emperor Theodosius the Great, hearing of his holiness, asked for his prayers before a battle, and that Sennouphios sent him his worn cloak and staff, by which the emperor was victorious.

He reposed in peace, and his memory is kept on March 25.
3-25.desc: Venerable Sennouphios the Sign-Bearer of Egypt.
3-25.name: Sennouphios the Sign-Bearer

3-25.bio:
Sts. Pelagia and Theodosia are martyrs whose names the Greek synaxaria record together for March 25, the feast of the Annunciation. Tradition relates that they confessed Christ and were put to death for the faith.

The Church keeps their memory on this day.
3-25.name: Pelagia and Theodosia

3-25.bio:
St. Demios is a martyr whose name the Greek synaxaria record for March 25 with the note that he completed his witness by the sword. Nothing further of his life has been preserved.

The Church keeps his memory on this day.
3-25.name: Demios the Martyr

3-25.bio:
St. Timon was a monk of Russia in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, a disciple of the elder Seraphim of Sarov according to tradition, who restored the hermitage of Nadeevo in the forests of Kostroma. He lived in great poverty and prayer, and reposed in 1840.

His memory is kept on March 25.
3-25.desc: Venerable Timon the Hermit of Nadeevo in Russia.
3-25.name: Timon the Hermit

3-25.bio:
St. Parthenios was a hieroschemamonk of the Kiev Caves Lavra in the nineteenth century, known for his unceasing prayer, his reading of the whole Psalter daily, and his gift of spiritual counsel. He reposed in 1855, on the feast of the Annunciation.

He was glorified by the Ukrainian Church, and his memory is kept on March 25.
3-25.desc: Venerable Parthenios of the Kiev Caves, hieroschemamonk.
3-25.name: Parthenios of Kiev

3-26.bio:
On the day after the Annunciation, the Church gathers in synaxis to honor the Archangel Gabriel, the messenger of the Incarnation. It was Gabriel who announced the conception of St. John the Forerunner to Zacharias, and above all who brought the Virgin Mary the good tidings that she would bear the Saviour of the world.

In Scripture and tradition Gabriel appears at the turning points of salvation history as the herald of divine mysteries. The faithful seek his intercession as one of the chief commanders of the heavenly hosts, honored again with the Archangel Michael on November 8.
3-26.desc: Synaxis of the Holy Archangel Gabriel, the day after the Annunciation.
3-26.name: Synaxis of the Archangel Gabriel

3-26.bio:
Sts. Kodratos, Theodosios and Manuel, with forty companions, were Christians of Anatolia who, according to tradition, were captured and pressed to renounce Christ. They confessed the faith steadfastly and were put to the sword.

The Church honors the whole company on March 26.
3-26.desc: Holy Martyrs Kodratos, Theodosios, Manuel and forty others of Anatolia.
3-26.name: Kodratos, Theodosios and Manuel

3-26.bio:
The twenty-six martyrs of Gothia were Christians of the Gothic people in the Crimea and beyond the Danube who suffered in the fourth century under the pagan king Athanaric. Tradition relates that they were burned to death in a church where they had gathered for the Liturgy, and that their relics were later brought to Cyzicus by a Gothic princess.

The Church keeps their memory on March 26.
3-26.desc: The Twenty-Six Holy Martyrs who suffered in Gothia.
3-26.name: Twenty-Six Martyrs of Gothia

3-26.bio:
St. Stephen was abbot of the monastery of Triglia in Bithynia in the ninth century. For his defense of the holy icons under the iconoclast emperor Leo the Armenian he was imprisoned and exiled, and reposed in exile after much suffering.

The Church honors him as a confessor on March 26.
3-26.desc: Venerable Stephen the Confessor, abbot of Triglia.
3-26.name: Stephen of Triglia

3-26.bio:
St. Basil the New was an ascetic of the tenth century who lived near Constantinople. Tradition relates that he was arrested as a suspected spy and tortured, but was released and thereafter lived in the city, known for his gift of foresight and his miracles. The vision of the aerial toll-houses associated with his disciple Gregory is recorded in his life.

He reposed in peace at a great age, and his memory is kept on March 26.
3-26.desc: Venerable Basil the New, anchorite near Constantinople.
3-26.name: Basil the New

3-26.bio:
St. George was a young Christian of Sofia in Bulgaria who lived under Ottoman rule. Tradition relates that he was pressed to accept Islam and, refusing steadfastly, was burned to death in 1515.

He is numbered among the New Martyrs of Bulgaria, and his memory is kept on March 26.
3-26.desc: Holy New Martyr George of Sofia, burned for the faith.
3-26.name: George of Sofia

3-27.bio:
St. Matrona was a servant in Thessaloniki in the early centuries of the Church, a Christian in the household of a pagan-hearted mistress who hated her faith. Slipping away in secret to pray with the Church, she was discovered, beaten, and confined, yet she would not abandon Christ, and she died of the cruel treatment she received, a true martyr.

The Christians of Thessaloniki honored her from ancient times, and her memory endures as a witness that no station in life is too lowly for sanctity. She is commemorated on March 27.
3-27.name: Matrona of Thessaloniki

3-27.bio:
St. Philetos was a senator of Rome who, with his wife Lydia and their sons Theoprepios and Makedon, suffered under the emperor Hadrian. Tradition relates that they were sent to Illyria, where the governor Amphilochios, converted by their steadfastness, was martyred with them, together with the jailer Kronides.

They were cast into boiling oil but were preserved unharmed, and reposed in the Lord soon after. The Church keeps their memory on March 27.
3-27.desc: Holy Martyrs Philetos the Senator, his wife Lydia, their sons Theoprepios and Makedon, and companions.
3-27.name: Philetos and Lydia

3-27.bio:
St. Kirykos is a venerable father of Apros in Thrace whose name the Greek synaxaria record for March 27 with the note that he reposed in peace. Nothing further of his life has been preserved.

The Church honors him on this day.
3-27.desc: Venerable Kirykos of Apros in Thrace.
3-27.name: Kirykos of Apros

3-27.bio:
St. Paul was Bishop of Corinth in the tenth century, the brother of St. Peter of Argos. Tradition relates that he was a man of learning and holiness who shepherded the Church of Corinth with wisdom and reposed in peace.

His memory is kept on March 27.
3-27.desc: Saint Paul, Bishop of Corinth, brother of Saint Peter of Argos.
3-27.name: Paul of Corinth

3-27.bio:
The prophet Hanani appears in the Old Testament as a seer in the days of King Asa of Judah. Because he rebuked the king for relying on the king of Syria rather than on the Lord, he was put in prison, as the Second Book of Chronicles relates.

The Church keeps his memory on March 27.
3-27.desc: Holy Prophet Hanani, the seer who rebuked King Asa.
3-27.name: Hanani the Prophet

3-27.bio:
Sts. John and Barouchios are martyrs whose names the Greek synaxaria record together for March 27. Tradition relates that they confessed Christ and were put to death by the sword.

The Church keeps their memory on this day.
3-27.name: John and Barouchios

3-28.bio:
St. Hilarion the New was abbot of the monastery of Pelekete in Asia Minor during the age of iconoclasm. A man of fasting, vigil, and deep humility, he guided his brotherhood in the monastic life and stood firm in the veneration of the holy icons when the emperors sought to abolish it.

For this confession he and his monastery suffered persecution, and he is numbered among the confessors who preserved the fullness of the faith for the generations after them. He is commemorated on March 28.
3-28.desc: Venerable Hilarion the New, Abbot of Pelekete.
3-28.name: Hilarion the New

3-28.bio:
St. Herodion was one of the Seventy Apostles, greeted by St. Paul as his kinsman in the Epistle to the Romans. Tradition relates that he was made Bishop of Neopatras in Greece, where he suffered much from the pagans, and that he later accompanied St. Peter to Rome and was martyred there.

The Greek synaxarion keeps his memory on March 28 and also on April 8.
3-28.desc: Holy Apostle Herodion of the Seventy, kinsman of Saint Paul.
3-28.name: Herodion the Apostle

3-28.bio:
St. Gabrielia was born Avrilia Papayianni in Constantinople in 1897 and trained as a physiotherapist in England. After the death of her mother she gave away everything and went to India, where she cared for lepers and the poor for years, and later was tonsured a nun in Jerusalem, living a life of hidden service in Greece, Africa, Europe and America.

She spent her last years on the island of Leros, where she reposed in 1992. Her sayings, gathered in the book The Ascetic of Love, are widely read. She was glorified by the Ecumenical Patriarchate in 2023, and her memory is kept on March 28.
3-28.desc: Venerable Gabrielia (Papayianni) of Constantinople, the ascetic of love, who reposed on Leros.
3-28.name: Gabrielia of Leros

3-28.bio:
St. Stephen the Wonderworker is a venerable father whom the Greek synaxaria commemorate on March 28 with the note that he reposed in peace. Nothing further of his life has been preserved.

The Church honors him on this day.
3-28.desc: Venerable Stephen the Wonderworker, who reposed in peace.
3-28.name: Stephen the Wonderworker

3-28.bio:
St. Eustratios was a monk of the Kiev Caves who was taken captive by the Cumans in 1096 and sold as a slave to a Jew of Cherson. Tradition relates that his master starved his captives to force them to renounce Christ, and that Eustratios, who alone survived because of his long practice of fasting, was crucified on the day of Pascha.

His body was cast into the sea and later found by the faithful; his relics rest in the Near Caves of the Lavra. His memory is kept on March 28.
3-28.desc: Holy Monk-Martyr Eustratios the Faster of the Kiev Caves, crucified for Christ.
3-28.name: Eustratios of the Kiev Caves

3-28.bio:
St. Hesychios was a presbyter of Jerusalem in the fifth century, a disciple according to tradition of St. Gregory the Theologian, and a renowned teacher and interpreter of Scripture. Writings on watchfulness and prayer attributed to Hesychios are included in the Philokalia and have been read by monastics through the centuries.

He reposed in peace, and the Church keeps his memory on March 28.
3-28.desc: Venerable Hesychios the Presbyter of Jerusalem, spiritual writer.
3-28.name: Hesychios of Jerusalem

3-28.bio:
St. Boyan, called Enravota, was the eldest son of the Bulgarian khan Omurtag in the ninth century. Converted to Christ through a Byzantine captive, he was disinherited and, when he refused to renounce the faith, was beheaded on the order of his brother, the khan Malamir, around the year 833.

He is honored as the first martyr of the Bulgarian people, and his memory is kept on March 28.
3-28.desc: Holy Martyr Boyan (Enravota), Prince of Bulgaria, first martyr of the Bulgarian people.
3-28.name: Boyan of Bulgaria

3-29.bio:
St. Mark was Bishop of Arethusa in Syria in the fourth century. In the days of Constantine he had destroyed a pagan temple and built up the Church; when Julian the Apostate restored idolatry, the aged bishop was seized by the pagans of the city and subjected to prolonged and vicious torments, which he endured with such meekness that even his tormentors marveled.

His patience under suffering became famous throughout the Church, and the fathers held him up as a model of forgiveness toward persecutors. He is commemorated on March 29.
3-29.name: Mark, Bishop of Arethusa

3-29.bio:
St. Savvas the New was born in Thrace in 1862 and became a monk on Mount Athos and in the Holy Land, where he practiced iconography and lived in great austerity. Returning to Greece, he became the spiritual father of St. Nektarios of Aegina and, after his elder's repose, settled at the convent of All Saints on the island of Kalymnos.

There he served the nuns and the islanders with love until his repose in 1948; his relics were found incorrupt. His memory is kept on March 29 and also on the fifth Sunday of Great Lent.
3-29.desc: Venerable Savvas the New of Kalymnos, iconographer and confessor.
3-29.name: Savvas of Kalymnos

3-29.bio:
St. Cyril was a deacon of Heliopolis in Phoenicia who, in the reign of Constantine, had broken idols in the city. When Julian the Apostate restored paganism, the pagans seized him and, according to tradition, tore open his body in their rage. At the same time, in Ascalon and Gaza in Palestine, consecrated virgins and priests were put to death with great cruelty.

The Church keeps their memory on March 29, together with St. Mark of Arethusa.
3-29.desc: Holy Martyr Cyril the Deacon of Heliopolis, and the martyrs of Ascalon and Gaza.
3-29.name: Cyril the Deacon

3-29.bio:
Sts. Jonah and Barachesios were monks of Persia in the fourth century who, during the persecution of King Shapur II, went to encourage a group of imprisoned Christians and were themselves arrested. They endured horrible tortures with great patience and were put to death, together with the martyrs Zanithas, Lazarus, Maruthas, Narses, Elias, Mares, Habib, Sembeeth and Sabas.

The Church keeps their memory on March 29.
3-29.desc: Holy Martyrs Jonah and Barachesios and their companions in Persia.
3-29.name: Jonah and Barachesios

3-29.bio:
St. Diadochos was Bishop of Photike in Epirus in the fifth century and one of the great teachers of the spiritual life. His work of one hundred chapters On Spiritual Knowledge, included in the Philokalia, teaches the remembrance of God and the invocation of the name of Jesus, and was read by St. Maximos the Confessor and many later fathers.

He took part in the defense of the Council of Chalcedon and reposed in peace. His memory is kept on March 29.
3-29.desc: Saint Diadochos, Bishop of Photike in Epirus, spiritual writer.
3-29.name: Diadochos of Photike

3-29.bio:
St. Eustathios was Bishop of Kios in Bithynia in the ninth century. For his defense of the holy icons he was persecuted by the iconoclasts, deprived of his see and subjected to hunger and exile.

He reposed after many years of suffering, and the Church honors him as a confessor on March 29.
3-29.desc: Saint Eustathios the Confessor, Bishop of Kios in Bithynia.
3-29.name: Eustathios of Kios

3-3.bio:
St. Hesychios was a martyr of Antioch who suffered during the Roman persecutions of the early fourth century. Tradition remembers him as a man of rank who, when the emperor demanded that Christians in imperial service deny their faith or lose their honors, laid aside his dignities rather than deny Christ, and was put to death for his confession.

The synaxaria preserve little else of his life, but his choice of Christ over every earthly honor has kept his memory alive in the Church. He is commemorated on March 3.
3-3.name: Hesychios

3-3.bio:
Sts. Eutropios, Kleonikos and Basiliskos were soldiers of Amasea in Pontus and companions of the Great Martyr Theodore the Recruit. Imprisoned after St. Theodore's martyrdom, they were tortured for refusing to sacrifice to idols; Eutropios and Kleonikos were crucified, while Basiliskos was kept in prison and later beheaded.

The Church honors the three together on March 3.
3-3.desc: Holy Martyrs Eutropios, Kleonikos and Basiliskos of Amasea.
3-3.name: Eutropios, Kleonikos and Basiliskos

3-3.bio:
St. Theodoretos was a presbyter of the Church of Antioch in the fourth century, entrusted with the care of the sacred vessels. When Julian the Apostate's uncle, also named Julian, plundered the great church of Antioch and demanded its treasures, Theodoretos refused to hand them over and boldly rebuked him.

He was tortured and beheaded for his confession, and tradition relates that his persecutor soon died of a terrible illness. The Church keeps his memory on March 3.
3-3.desc: Hieromartyr Theodoretos, presbyter of Antioch, who suffered under Julian.
3-3.name: Theodoretos of Antioch

3-3.bio:
Sts. Zenon and Zoilos are venerable fathers whose names the Greek synaxaria record for March 3 with the simple note that they reposed in peace. Nothing further of their lives has been preserved.

The Church keeps their memory together on this day.
3-3.desc: Venerable Zenon and Zoilos, who reposed in peace.
3-3.name: Zenon and Zoilos

3-3.bio:
St. Piamoun was a virgin of Egypt in the fourth century who lived in her mother's house in strict asceticism, spinning flax and eating only every other day. Tradition relates that she received the gift of foresight and once, through her prayers, held back armed men who were coming to attack her village during a dispute over water.

She reposed in peace, and the Church honors her on March 3.
3-3.desc: Venerable Piamoun the Virgin of Egypt.
3-3.name: Piamoun the Virgin

3-3.bio:
St. Alexandra was a virgin of Alexandria in the fourth century who, in order to avoid being a cause of temptation to a young man, shut herself in a tomb and lived there for many years in prayer, receiving food through a small opening. Her story is told by Palladius in the Lausiac History.

She reposed in peace, and the Church honors her on March 3.
3-3.desc: Venerable Alexandra of Alexandria, who lived enclosed in a tomb.
3-3.name: Alexandra of Alexandria

3-30.bio:
St. John Climacus came to Mount Sinai as a young man and spent his whole life there, first in obedience to an elder, then in long years of stillness in the desert, and finally as abbot of the great monastery of Sinai. At the request of another abbot he wrote The Ladder of Divine Ascent, describing thirty steps of the spiritual life leading from renunciation to love.

The Ladder became one of the most beloved books of Orthodox spirituality, read in monasteries every Great Lent. He is commemorated on March 30 and on the fourth Sunday of the Fast.
3-30.desc: Venerable John Climacus, author of The Ladder of Divine Ascent.
3-30.name: John Climacus

3-30.bio:
St. Zacharias was Metropolitan of Corinth in the seventeenth century. Falsely accused before the Ottoman authorities of stirring up the people against the sultan, he was pressed to accept Islam and, refusing, was tortured and beheaded in 1684 according to the synaxaria.

He is honored as a hieromartyr, and his memory is kept on March 30.
3-30.desc: Hieromartyr Zacharias, Metropolitan of Corinth, beheaded by the Ottomans.
3-30.name: Zacharias of Corinth

3-30.bio:
St. John was Patriarch of Jerusalem in the early centuries of the Church, remembered in the Greek synaxaria as a holy hierarch who governed the Mother of Churches with wisdom and reposed in peace.

His memory is kept on March 30.
3-30.name: John of Jerusalem

3-30.bio:
St. Euboule was the mother of the Great Martyr Panteleimon, a Christian woman of Nicomedia married to a pagan husband. She raised her son in the faith from childhood, and though she reposed before his martyrdom, the seeds she planted bore fruit when he returned to Christ and became the unmercenary physician and martyr honored throughout the Church.

Her memory is kept on March 30.
3-30.desc: Righteous Euboule, mother of the Great Martyr Panteleimon.
3-30.name: Euboule

3-30.bio:
St. Viktor is a martyr whose name the Greek synaxaria record for March 30 with the note that he completed his witness by the sword. Nothing further of his life has been preserved.

The Church keeps his memory on this day.
3-30.name: Viktor the Martyr

3-30.bio:
St. Sophronios was born in Ukraine in 1704 and became a monk and abbot before being consecrated Bishop of Irkutsk in eastern Siberia in 1753. He traveled through his vast diocese, preaching to the native peoples, building churches and schools, and caring for the poor.

He reposed in 1771 and was glorified in 1918. His memory is kept on March 30.
3-30.desc: Saint Sophronios, Bishop of Irkutsk, missionary of Siberia.
3-30.name: Sophronios of Irkutsk

3-31.bio:
St. Hypatius was Bishop of Gangra in Paphlagonia in the fourth century and a father of the First Ecumenical Council at Nicaea, where the divinity of Christ was confessed against Arius. A wonderworker famed for his prayers, he shepherded his flock with zeal against every heresy.

Tradition relates that he was ambushed by heretics on a mountain road and mortally wounded, dying with prayer for his attackers, so that the Church honors him as both hierarch and martyr. He is commemorated on March 31.
3-31.desc: Hieromartyr Hypatius the Wonderworker, Bishop of Gangra.
3-31.name: Hypatius, Bishop of Gangra

3-31.bio:
St. Akakios was Bishop of Melitene in Armenia in the third century. During the persecution of Decius he was arrested and brought before the governor, whom he answered with such wisdom that the emperor, on reading the record of the trial, ordered his release.

He returned to his flock and reposed in peace, honored as a confessor. His memory is kept on March 31.
3-31.desc: Saint Akakios the Confessor, Bishop of Melitene.
3-31.name: Akakios of Melitene

3-31.bio:
St. Abdas was a bishop in Persia in the fifth century who was put to death by King Yazdegerd after he destroyed a fire temple of the Zoroastrians and refused to rebuild it. His deacon Benjamin was imprisoned, released on condition that he stop preaching, and, continuing to preach Christ, was tortured and killed.

The Church keeps their memory on March 31.
3-31.desc: Hieromartyr Abdas, Bishop of Persia, and Martyr Benjamin the Deacon.
3-31.name: Abdas and Benjamin

3-31.bio:
St. Theophilos and his companions were martyrs of Crete whose names the Greek synaxaria record for March 31. Tradition relates that they confessed Christ before the pagan authorities of the island and were put to death for the faith.

The Church keeps their memory on this day.
3-31.desc: Holy Martyr Theophilos and those who suffered with him in Crete.
3-31.name: Theophilos of Crete

3-31.bio:
St. Menandros is a martyr whose name the Greek synaxaria record for March 31 with the note that he was put to death by being dragged over sharp stones for his confession of Christ. Nothing further of his life has been preserved.

The Church keeps his memory on this day.
3-31.name: Menandros the Martyr

3-31.bio:
St. Blasios was born near Amorion in Phrygia in the ninth century and became a monk in Constantinople, later traveling to Rome, where he lived for many years in a Greek monastery. Returning to Constantinople, he lived at the Studion monastery and finally on Mount Athos, where he founded a monastery and reposed in peace.

His memory is kept on March 31.
3-31.desc: Venerable Blasios of Amorion, monk of Studion and Mount Athos.
3-31.name: Blasios of Amorion

3-31.bio:
St. Innocent (Veniaminov) was born in Siberia in 1797 and as a young married priest volunteered for the mission in Alaska. He labored for decades among the Aleuts, Tlingit and other native peoples, learning their languages, translating the Scriptures and services, and building churches, and after the death of his wife was consecrated bishop for the Alaskan mission.

In 1868 he was elected Metropolitan of Moscow, where he founded the Orthodox Missionary Society. He reposed in 1879 and was glorified in 1977 as the apostle to America. His memory is kept on March 31.
3-31.desc: Saint Innocent, Metropolitan of Moscow, enlightener of Alaska and apostle to America.
3-31.name: Innocent of Alaska

3-4.bio:
St. Gerasimos was a fifth-century ascetic who founded a great monastery in the desert by the River Jordan, guiding many monks in a strict rule of poverty, silence, and prayer, and was counted among the great elders of the Palestinian desert.

He is best remembered for the lion who, according to tradition, was healed by the saint of a thorn in its paw and thereafter served him tamely until his death — an image of paradise restored around a man of God. The Church commemorates him on March 4.
3-4.desc: Venerable Gerasimos of the Jordan who tamed a lion.
3-4.name: Gerasimos of the Jordan

3-4.bio:
Sts. Paul and Juliana were brother and sister from Ptolemais in Phoenicia who suffered under the emperor Aurelian in the third century. Arrested for confessing Christ, they endured cruel tortures; tradition relates that several of their guards, among them Stratonikos, Kodratos and Akakios, were converted by their steadfastness and were martyred with them.

All were beheaded, and the Church keeps their memory on March 4.
3-4.desc: Holy Martyrs Paul and his sister Juliana of Ptolemais, with Stratonikos and companions.
3-4.name: Paul and Juliana

3-4.bio:
St. Gregory was Bishop of Constantia (ancient Salamis) in Cyprus, remembered in the Greek synaxaria together with St. Adrianos. Tradition relates that he shepherded his flock with wisdom and reposed in peace.

The Church keeps their memory on March 4.
3-4.desc: Saint Gregory, Bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, with Saint Adrianos.
3-4.name: Gregory of Constantia and Adrianos

3-4.bio:
St. Gregory was born on the island of Lesbos and became Bishop of Assos on the coast of Asia Minor, probably in the twelfth century. Tradition relates that he was a man of great humility and prayer who, driven from his see by slander, returned to Lesbos and founded a monastery, where he reposed in peace.

He is venerated especially on Lesbos, and his memory is kept on March 4.
3-4.desc: Saint Gregory, Bishop of Assos in Asia Minor, wonderworker.
3-4.name: Gregory of Assos

3-4.bio:
St. Daniel was the youngest son of St. Alexander Nevsky and the first prince of Moscow, living in the second half of the thirteenth century. He ruled with gentleness, avoiding bloodshed among the quarreling princes, and founded the monastery near Moscow that still bears his name.

Before his death in 1303 he received the monastic tonsure. He is honored as a righteous prince, and his memory is kept on March 4.
3-4.desc: Right-believing Prince Daniel of Moscow, youngest son of Saint Alexander Nevsky.
3-4.name: Daniel of Moscow

3-4.bio:
St. Gerasimos was a monk of Kiev who in the twelfth century traveled north to the forests of Vologda, where he built a church of the Holy Trinity and founded a monastery. Tradition relates that he was a hieromonk of great gentleness and that he labored among the settlers of the region until his repose in 1178.
