He is honored as one of the first monastic saints of the Russian north, and his memory is kept on March 4.
3-4.desc: Venerable Gerasimos of Vologda, founder of the Trinity Monastery.
3-4.name: Gerasimos of Vologda

3-4.bio:
St. Basil (Vasilko) was Prince of Rostov in the thirteenth century. Captured by the Mongols after the battle on the river Sit in 1238, he refused to renounce Christ or to serve the invaders, and was put to death.

His body was recovered and buried in the cathedral of Rostov. The Church honors him as a righteous prince and passion-bearer on March 4.
3-4.desc: Right-believing Prince Basil (Vasilko) of Rostov, martyred by the Mongols.
3-4.name: Basil of Rostov

3-5.bio:
St. Konon was an early martyr from Isauria in Asia Minor, remembered as a man of simple and holy life who drew many of his countrymen from idolatry to faith in Christ. When persecution reached his homeland, he confessed the Lord openly and endured torture at the hands of the pagans.

The faithful of Isauria honored him from ancient times as a wonderworker and intercessor, and his veneration spread through the Christian East. He is commemorated on March 5.
3-5.name: Konon

3-5.bio:
St. Savas the Sanctified was born in Cappadocia in the fifth century and came as a young man to the Judean desert, where he became a disciple of the great elders of Palestine. In the wild gorge of the Kidron he founded the Great Lavra, which still bears his name, and became the leader and lawgiver of the monks of the desert.

His order of services deeply shaped the worship of the whole Orthodox Church, and his monastery has remained a fountain of holiness for fifteen centuries. He reposed at a great age and is commemorated on March 5.
3-5.desc: Founder of the Great Lavra monastery in Palestine.
3-5.name: Savas the Sanctified

3-5.bio:
St. Konon the Gardener was a Christian of Nazareth who lived in Pamphylia, tending a garden and living simply from his labor. During the persecution of Decius he was arrested and, when he refused to sacrifice, nails were driven into his feet and he was forced to run before the governor's chariot until he collapsed.

He died praying, and the Church honors him on March 5, together with his namesake Konon of Isauria.
3-5.desc: Holy Martyr Konon the Gardener of Pamphylia.
3-5.name: Konon the Gardener

3-5.bio:
St. Mark the Ascetic lived in the fourth and fifth centuries, a disciple of St. John Chrysostom according to tradition, and spent many years in the deserts of Egypt. He is best known for his spiritual writings, several of which are preserved in the Philokalia, including the treatises On the Spiritual Law and On Those Who Think They Are Justified by Works.

Tradition relates that he knew the Scriptures by heart and was famed for his meekness. He reposed in peace at a great age, and his memory is kept on March 5.
3-5.desc: Venerable Mark the Ascetic, spiritual writer of the Philokalia.
3-5.name: Mark the Ascetic

3-5.bio:
St. George was born in the village of Rapsani near Mount Olympus in Thessaly and lived under Ottoman rule. Tradition relates that he was accused before the Turkish authorities at Tyrnavos and pressed to accept Islam, but refused steadfastly and was put to death in 1818.

He is numbered among the New Martyrs of Greece, and his memory is kept on March 5.
3-5.desc: Holy New Martyr George of Rapsani in Thessaly.
3-5.name: George of Rapsani

3-5.bio:
Sts. Eulogios and Eulampios were martyrs of Palestine whose names the Greek synaxaria record together for March 5. Tradition relates that Eulogios, a Christian of Palestine, preached Christ boldly to the pagans and was beheaded, and that Eulampios also completed his witness by the sword.

The Church keeps their memory on March 5.
3-5.desc: Holy Martyrs Eulogios and Eulampios of Palestine.
3-5.name: Eulogios and Eulampios

3-5.bio:
St. Archelaos and the one hundred fifty-two martyrs with him are commemorated in the Greek synaxaria for March 5. Tradition relates that they confessed Christ together and were put to the sword.

Nothing further of their lives has been preserved, but the Church honors the whole company on this day.
3-5.desc: Holy Martyr Archelaos and the 152 martyrs with him.
3-5.name: Archelaos and 152 Martyrs

3-5.bio:
St. Nicholas Velimirovich was born in Serbia in 1880 and became one of the most gifted preachers and writers of the Orthodox Church in the twentieth century, serving as Bishop of Ochrid and later of Zicha. During the Second World War he was imprisoned by the Germans and held in the Dachau concentration camp; after the war he lived in exile in the United States, teaching and writing until his repose in 1956.

Among his many works is the Prologue from Ochrid, a daily book of saints' lives and reflections. He was glorified by the Serbian Church in 2003, and the Greek synaxarion keeps his memory on March 5.
3-5.desc: Saint Nicholas (Velimirovich), Bishop of Ochrid and Zicha, the new Chrysostom of Serbia.
3-5.name: Nicholas of Zicha

3-6.bio:
The Forty-Two Martyrs of Amorium were Byzantine officers taken captive when the city of Amorium in Asia Minor fell to the Arabs in the year 838. Held in harsh imprisonment for some seven years, they were pressed again and again to abandon Christ and accept the faith of their captors, with freedom and honors promised if they yielded.

Every one of them refused, and they were beheaded together by the river Euphrates in 845. The Church honors their long, unbroken confession, sealed after years of suffering, and commemorates them on March 6.
3-6.desc: The Forty-Two Holy Martyrs of Amorium.
3-6.name: Forty-Two Martyrs of Amorium

3-6.bio:
On this day the Church remembers the finding of the Precious Cross of the Lord and of the Holy Nails in Jerusalem by St. Helen, mother of St. Constantine the Great, in the fourth century. Tradition relates that three crosses were uncovered near Golgotha and that the true Cross was recognized when a dying woman was healed by its touch.

The Cross was raised before the people by Patriarch Makarios of Jerusalem, an event celebrated more fully on September 14. The finding itself is commemorated on March 6.
3-6.desc: Commemoration of the finding of the Precious Cross and the Holy Nails by Saint Helen.
3-6.name: Finding of the Precious Cross

3-6.bio:
St. Hesychios was an ascetic of Bithynia in the eighth century who settled on a mountain near Andrapa, building a small cell and a church of St. Andrew. Tradition relates that he lived in fasting and prayer, that he was granted the gift of working miracles, and that he foretold the day of his own repose.

His relics were later translated to Amasea. His memory is kept on March 6.
3-6.desc: Venerable Hesychios the Wonderworker of Bithynia, the Faster.
3-6.name: Hesychios the Wonderworker

3-6.bio:
St. Arkadios was Archbishop of Cyprus in the seventh century, in the years when the island faced the first Arab raids. Tradition relates that he was a learned and pastoral bishop who defended the Orthodox faith and cared for his flock in a time of trial.

He reposed in peace, and the Church of Cyprus keeps his memory on March 6.
3-6.name: Arkadios of Cyprus

3-6.bio:
St. Maximos was a monk whose name the Greek synaxaria preserve for March 6 with the note that he was stoned to death for his confession of Christ. Nothing further of his life has come down to us.

The Church honors him among the monk-martyrs on this day.
3-6.desc: Holy Monk-Martyr Maximos, stoned for the faith.
3-6.name: Maximos the Monk-Martyr

3-6.bio:
Sts. Julian and Euboulos were martyrs whose memory the Greek synaxaria keep on March 6. Tradition relates that they confessed Christ before the pagan authorities and were put to death by the sword.

The Church commemorates them together on this day.
3-6.name: Julian and Euboulos

3-7.bio:
St. Ephraim was one of the holy bishops sent in the early fourth century to preach the Gospel in Cherson on the Black Sea, a region still in the grip of paganism. Together with his fellow hieromartyr bishops of Cherson, he labored to plant the faith among a hostile people, and sealed his preaching with his blood.

The Church remembers these missionary bishops together as founders of the Church in that land, their sacrifice bearing fruit in generations of believers. St. Ephraim is commemorated on March 7.
3-7.desc: Holy Hieromartyrs and Bishops of Cherson.
3-7.name: Ephraim, Bishop of Cherson

3-7.bio:
The hieromartyrs of Cherson were bishops sent in the fourth century by the Patriarch of Jerusalem to preach the Gospel in Cherson in the Crimea, together with St. Ephraim. Basileus, Eugenios, Agathodoros, Elpidios, Kapiton and Aitherios labored there one after another among the pagans of the region, and most of them were put to death by the unbelievers.

Tradition relates that St. Kapiton confirmed the faith before the people by passing unharmed through a fiery furnace. The Church honors the seven bishops of Cherson together on March 7.
3-7.desc: Hieromartyrs Basileus, Eugenios, Agathodoros, Elpidios, Kapiton and Aitherios, bishops of Cherson.
3-7.name: Hieromartyrs of Cherson

3-7.bio:
St. Paul the Simple was a farmer of Egypt in the fourth century who, at the age of sixty, left his unfaithful wife and went into the desert to become a disciple of St. Anthony the Great. Anthony tested his patience with many hard tasks, and Paul obeyed everything with such simplicity and humility that he soon received the gift of casting out demons.

Tradition relates that he could heal cases which even St. Anthony had not been able to cure. He reposed in peace, and his memory is kept on March 7.
3-7.desc: Venerable Paul the Simple, disciple of Saint Anthony the Great.
3-7.name: Paul the Simple

3-7.bio:
St. Ephraim was a civil governor of the East who, after helping to rebuild Antioch following a great earthquake, was chosen Patriarch of that city in the sixth century. He defended the doctrine of the Council of Chalcedon against the Monophysites and wrote many works in defense of the Orthodox faith.

Tradition relates that he once proved the truth of his confession by having his stole cast into a fire, from which it was drawn unharmed. He reposed in peace, and his memory is kept on March 7.
3-7.desc: Saint Ephraim, Patriarch of Antioch, defender of Chalcedon.
3-7.name: Ephraim of Antioch

3-7.bio:
St. Lavrentios was born in Megara in the seventeenth century, a married man and father who, after a vision of the Mother of God, crossed to the island of Salamis and found her ancient icon buried in a ruined church. There he founded the monastery of the Panagia Phaneromeni, which remains a place of pilgrimage.

He was tonsured a monk and reposed in peace in 1707. His memory is kept on March 7.
3-7.desc: Venerable Lavrentios, founder of the Monastery of Phaneromeni on Salamis.
3-7.name: Lavrentios of Salamis

3-7.bio:
Sts. Arkadios and Nestor were bishops of Trimythous in Cyprus, the see later made famous by St. Spyridon. Tradition relates that they lived in the early centuries of the Church on the island and shepherded their flocks in holiness.

They reposed in peace, and the Church of Cyprus keeps their memory together on March 7.
3-7.desc: Saints Arkadios and Nestor, Bishops of Trimythous in Cyprus.
3-7.name: Arkadios and Nestor of Trimythous

3-7.bio:
St. Aimilianos was a Christian of Rome, remembered in the Greek synaxaria together with Sts. Jacob and Marianos. Tradition relates that they confessed Christ during the persecutions and were put to death for their faith.

The Church keeps their memory on March 7.
3-7.desc: Holy Martyr Aimilianos of Rome, with Jacob and Marianos.
3-7.name: Aimilianos of Rome

3-8.bio:
The holy Prophet Zacharias was a priest of the Temple in Jerusalem and the father of St. John the Forerunner. As the Gospel of Luke relates, the Archangel Gabriel appeared to him at the altar of incense and announced that his aged wife Elizabeth would bear a son; when John was born, Zacharias was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied of the dawn from on high.

Tradition honors him as both prophet and martyr, holding that he was slain in the Temple for his faithfulness to God. He is commemorated on March 8.
3-8.desc: Prophet Zacharias, father of John the Baptist.
3-8.name: Zacharias

3-8.bio:
St. Theophylaktos was a monk and disciple of St. Tarasios, Patriarch of Constantinople, who made him Bishop of Nicomedia in the late eighth century. There he built churches and hospices, cared for the poor and the sick with his own hands, and governed his flock with great charity.

When the emperor Leo the Armenian revived iconoclasm, Theophylaktos boldly rebuked him and was sent into exile, where he reposed after some thirty years. The Church honors him as a confessor on March 8.
3-8.desc: Saint Theophylaktos, Bishop of Nicomedia, confessor against iconoclasm.
3-8.name: Theophylaktos of Nicomedia

3-8.bio:
St. Paul was Bishop of Plousias in Bithynia in the ninth century, during the second period of iconoclasm. For his defense of the holy icons he was persecuted, driven from his see and subjected to many hardships.

He reposed in exile, and the Church honors him as a confessor on March 8.
3-8.desc: Saint Paul the Confessor, Bishop of Plousias in Bithynia.
3-8.name: Paul of Plousias

3-8.bio:
St. Hermes was one of the Seventy Apostles, greeted by St. Paul in his Epistle to the Romans. Tradition relates that he became Bishop of Dalmatia and labored there in preaching the Gospel.

The Greek synaxarion keeps his memory on March 8, and he is also commemorated with the Seventy on January 4.
3-8.desc: Holy Apostle Hermes of the Seventy, greeted by Saint Paul in the Epistle to the Romans.
3-8.name: Hermes the Apostle

3-8.bio:
St. Dion was a martyr of the early Church whose name is recorded in the Greek synaxaria for March 8 with the note that he completed his witness by the sword. Nothing further of his life has been preserved.

The Church keeps his memory on this day.
3-8.name: Dion the Martyr

3-8.bio:
St. Dometios is a venerable father whose name the Greek synaxaria record for March 8 with the simple note that he reposed in peace. Nothing further of his life has come down to us.

The Church honors him on this day.
3-8.desc: Venerable Dometios, ascetic who reposed in peace.
3-8.name: Dometios the Venerable

3-8.bio:
On this day the Church of Laconia in the Peloponnese gathers in one commemoration all the saints who were born, labored or were martyred in that region, from the early centuries through the New Martyrs of the Ottoman period.

The synaxis was established in recent years by the local metropolis and is kept on March 8.
3-8.desc: Synaxis of all the saints who shone forth in Laconia.
3-8.name: Synaxis of the Saints of Laconia

3-9.bio:
The Forty Holy Martyrs of Sebaste were Roman soldiers who confessed Christ in Armenia in the year 320, during the persecution of Licinius. Refusing to deny the Lord, they were condemned to stand through the night upon a frozen lake, with warm baths set on the shore to tempt them. One gave way, but a guard, beholding crowns descending upon the martyrs, confessed Christ and took his place, completing the forty.

Their memory on March 9 is kept with love in the midst of the Great Fast, honored as an image of endurance to the end. In Greek tradition the day is the name day of Sarantis.
3-9.desc: The Forty Holy Martyrs who froze in the lake of Sebaste.
3-9.name: Forty Holy Martyrs of Sebaste

3-9.bio:
St. Ourpasianos was a senator of Nicomedia under the emperor Maximian. When the emperor demanded that Christians in his service renounce their faith, Ourpasianos laid down his belt of office before him and confessed Christ openly.

Tradition relates that he was shut in an iron cage and slowly burned to death, and that his ashes were scattered in the sea. The Church keeps his memory on March 9.
3-9.desc: Holy Martyr Ourpasianos of Nicomedia, burned in an iron cage.
3-9.name: Ourpasianos

3-9.bio:
St. Kaisarios was the younger brother of St. Gregory the Theologian, born in Cappadocia in the fourth century. Educated in Alexandria, he became a distinguished physician and served at the imperial court in Constantinople, keeping his Christian faith even under Julian the Apostate.

He survived a great earthquake at Nicaea and, moved by this deliverance, devoted himself wholly to God, but reposed soon after. St. Gregory delivered his funeral oration. The Church keeps his memory on March 9.
3-9.desc: Righteous Kaisarios, physician, brother of Saint Gregory the Theologian.
3-9.name: Kaisarios the Physician

3-9.bio:
St. Vitalios was born in Castronovo in Sicily in the tenth century and became a monk of the Greek monastery of St. Philip at Agira. He later lived as a hermit in various places in Sicily and Calabria, gathering disciples and founding monasteries, and was known for his miracles and his care for the poor.

He reposed in peace around the end of the tenth century, and his memory is kept on March 9.
3-9.desc: Venerable Vitalios of Castronovo in Sicily.
3-9.name: Vitalios of Sicily

3-9.bio:
Sts. Christos the priest and Panagos were New Martyrs of the Ottoman period commemorated in the Greek synaxaria on March 9. Tradition relates that they were seized by the Turkish authorities and put to death for refusing to deny the Christian faith.

The Church keeps their memory together on this day.
3-9.desc: Holy New Martyrs Christos the Priest and Panagos.
3-9.name: Christos and Panagos

3-9.bio:
The Greek synaxarion for March 9 records a whole household of martyrs, a grandfather and grandmother, a father and mother, and their two children, who confessed Christ together and were put to death for the faith. Their names have not been preserved.

The Church honors the family as one company of martyrs on this day.
3-9.desc: Holy Martyrs, a grandfather, grandmother, father, mother and their two children.
3-9.name: Six Martyrs of One Family
